1.pericope_label: I am the man that hath seen affliction: he hath led me into darkness, and set me in dark places as the dead of old
debates: Who the man of the first verse is
Whether the chapter may be applied to the passion of Christ
Whether the tripled acrostic is an improvement on the earlier chapters
outliers: Gill reads the sufferer throughout as a type of Christ, and Clarke says that such application of the poem is in his opinion without any foundation
Calvin rejects as improbable the view that the chapter was written while Jeremiah was in prison, holding that it was composed for the calamity of the whole people
Calvin judges the verses of this chapter needlessly multiplied and thinks one letter to a verse would have been better
themes: A name withheld while the hand is described
Anger distinguished as a rod and not a sword
An alphabet used three times over
A plea to be killed in the light rather than the dark

7.pericope_label: He hath hedged me about and made my chain heavy: he hath bent his bow and set me as a mark for the arrow
debates: Whether the confinement is the siege and the prison or a figure for distress generally
Why prayer is said to be shut out
What the turning aside of the ways means
outliers: Gill and Clarke both allow the wall of hewn stone to refer to the siege of the city, and Calvin says that view is not suitable to the passage at all
Calvin calls the shutting out of prayer strange and inconsistent with what Scripture everywhere promises, and answers that God hears in such a way as to try the patience of the faithful
themes: Fetters heavy enough to stop the feet lifting
Prayer stopped by the one it was addressed to
By-paths that twist and lead nowhere
A marksman who cannot miss and a butt that cannot move

13.pericope_label: He hath caused the arrows of his quiver to enter into my reins: I was a derision to all my people, and their song all the day
debates: Whether the derision is the prophet own experience or the nation
Whether the last word of the fifteenth verse is wormwood or poison
How the sons of the quiver is to be construed
outliers: Calvin denies that the word means wormwood, since wormwood though bitter is a wholesome herb, and takes it for poison or gall, against Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott who all keep it
Gill reports Aben Ezra reading my people as peoples, the surrounding nations, while Keil and Delitzsch refuse the plural and keep the singular
Clarke cites an Arabic poet who terms a grievously afflicted man a pounder of wormwood
themes: Arrows called the sons of the quiver
A sufferer mocked by the people he belongs to
Bread that is all grit and no flour
Peace so far off that prosperity is forgotten

19.pericope_label: Remembering mine affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the gall: this I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope
debates: Whether the verb of the nineteenth verse is an infinitive or an imperative prayer
Whether the verb of the twentieth verse is second person or third
Whether the pronoun this points back to what precedes or forward to what follows
outliers: Calvin refuses the common reference of the pronoun to the next verse, since a clause intervenes, and refers it back to the assurance that God would hear, against Henry, Wesley and Gill who all take it forward
Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering that makes the soul at rest, holding that the verb means to sink down and here to be bowed down
Calvin warns that those who fix their minds too much on the remembrance of their evils open the door to Satan, and urges a middle course in grief
themes: A prayer that opens by reciting the sufferings just complained of
A soul that presses down the man it ought to raise up
Humility reached before hope
Clouds beginning to disperse in the middle of a lament

22.pericope_label: It is of the mercies of the Lord that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not: they are new every morning
debates: Whether the first clause says that the faithful are not consumed or that the mercies have no end
Whether the mercies are renewed in God or only in the apprehension of men
What it means to call God a portion
outliers: Calvin sets aside the common rendering of the first clause and makes the mercies of Jehovah the subject, so that the sense is that they have no end
Calvin adds that the renewal is to be understood according to the apprehension of men, since to God belongs no change
Gill carries the promise of not being consumed from the remnant left for the Messiah to the principle of grace in the people of God, which he says can never be lost
themes: A centre of trust set between two stretches of lament
Blessings suspended through the night and renewed at dawn
A portion confessed by the soul and not only by the mouth
Affliction measured against what iniquity deserved

25.pericope_label: The Lord is good unto them that wait for him: it is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth
debates: Whether the yoke is the yoke of instruction or of chastisement
Whether the verses describe the patient man or command him
Whether the mention of youth dates the poem to the youth of Jeremiah
outliers: Ellicott rejects as a strange literalism the view that the mention of youth dates the poem to the youth of Jeremiah, hearing instead a man who looks back from the experience of age
Calvin allows both senses of the yoke but prefers obedience generally, where Clarke and Wesley take it of early discipline and Gill retains both
Keil and Delitzsch find a deliberate gradation in the three verses, the sitting alone being easiest and the giving of the cheek hardest
themes: Three consecutive lines that all begin with the word good
Patience proved where there is no witness to see it
A mouth laid in the dust and therefore unable to speak
Submission that must extend to injuries done by men

31.pericope_label: For the Lord will not cast off for ever: but though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies
debates: Whether the three infinitives depend on the clause that God does not afflict willingly or on the clause that the Lord approves not
Whether not from the heart can properly be said of God at all
Who the prisoners of the earth are
outliers: Calvin sets out both connections of the three infinitives and shows that they yield opposite ends, one an exhortation to patience and the other a ground of consolation
Clarke follows Blayney in taking the prisoners of the earth for insolvent debtors imprisoned until they work out the debt
Keil and Delitzsch refer the treading down of the prisoners to the treatment of the people at the taking of Jerusalem
themes: Three reasons joined by a threefold for
A God said to act unwillingly, and the impropriety of saying it
Injustice done in the very place where God is present
Punishment described as against the eternal will of God

37.pericope_label: Who is he that saith, and it cometh to pass, when the Lord commandeth it not? Wherefore doth a living man complain
debates: Whether the second verse is a question or a statement
What the verb of the last verse means
Whether the evil that proceeds from the mouth of God can include the evil of sin
outliers: Gill insists that the evils meant are judgments and chastisements only, the evil of sin coming not out of the mouth of God but standing under his permissive will
Calvin canvasses lying, murmuring and hardening as renderings of the last verb and prefers the sense of wearying oneself, from the word used of the people in Numbers
Keil and Delitzsch refuse the account of the transition that would turn the summons to search our ways into a prohibition of complaint
themes: A God imagined as idle, and the rebuke of that thought
Men as tools managed by a hand not their own
Life still lent as a reason not to complain
Judgment executed in silence where no prophet proclaims it

40.pericope_label: Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the Lord: we have transgressed and have rebelled, thou hast not pardoned
debates: What it means to say that God has not pardoned
Whether lifting the hands is the prayer or only its gesture
Where confession stands in the order of repentance
outliers: Henry calls the complaint that God has not pardoned a mistake, though a common one with the people of God when their souls are cast down, since the judgments were still on them and the assurance of pardon was wanting
Clarke notes that the alphabetical order of the verses just ahead is inverted, one letter standing where the other should
Calvin would render the confession with the pronoun emphatic, so that the faithful take on themselves the blame of all the evils which most men seek to disown
themes: A cover stripped off before the search begins
Prayer analysed from the will through the heart to the hands
Sin called by its two hardest names
A confession that must not be jejune or extorted

43.pericope_label: Thou hast covered thyself with a cloud, that our prayer should not pass through: thou hast made us as the offscouring and refuse in the midst of the people
debates: Whether it is God or the people that is covered with anger
What the sweepings and refuse in the midst of the peoples means
Whether one word of these verses has been mistranslated in an old version
outliers: Calvin holds that the severity of the complaint is not bitterness but a simple acknowledgment of righteous vengeance, since the temple was burnt and the kingdom overthrown
Calvin suspects a copyist error rather than a misread letter behind the rendering of one word as prophesying in the version of Jerome
Ellicott would render the word for desolation as devastation, the noun occurring nowhere else though its cognate verb is known
themes: Wrath worn as a garment
A cloud that prayer cannot get through
A nation swept up like the dirt of a floor
Reproach added to calamity as the bitterest part

49.pericope_label: Mine eye trickleth down, and ceaseth not: mine enemies chased me sore, like a bird, without cause
debates: Whether the sufferings from here to the end are the prophet own or the nation
Whether the stone was cast at him or laid over the mouth of the pit
Whether the daughters of the city are its maidens or its dependent towns
outliers: Calvin reads the preposition comparatively, so that the prophet wept more than all the daughters of the city and had almost forgotten his manhood
Calvin denies that stoning was meant and reads the stone as laid over the pit, as was done with Daniel, where Keil and Delitzsch argue from the verb that stones were cast at him
Keil and Delitzsch observe that the word chosen for enemies rather than the word for haters keeps the persecution from being reduced to private hatred
themes: Weeping that waits instead of weeping that despairs
An eye worn out by tears that then hurts the soul
Fowlers and a bird with neither prudence nor courage
A pit made into a grave by a stone

55.pericope_label: I called upon thy name, O Lord, out of the low dungeon: thou drewest near in the day that I called upon thee, thou saidst, Fear not
debates: Whether the low dungeon is literal or figurative
Whether the word rendered breathing means sighing or crying
Whether the wrong of the last verse is the wrong done to him or an ironical mention of his own iniquity
outliers: Calvin refuses the usual rendering of breathing and takes both words for crying, since in groaning the spirit dilates and the soul compressed by grief expands
Ellicott would refer the words historically to a particular rescue, the intervention of Ebed-melech
Calvin observes that friends who interpose for our defence do not always succeed, whereas God pleads a cause and delivers besides
themes: Faith getting the last word after complaint
A prayer too faint to be spoken aloud
Past answers used as grounds for present asking
An advocate who is also next of kin

61.pericope_label: Render unto them a recompence, O Lord, according to the work of their hands: persecute and destroy them in anger from under the heavens of the Lord
debates: Whether the closing verses are petitions or predictions
What the sorrow of heart is
Why the heavens of the Lord are named in the last line
outliers: Clarke holds the closing verses to be all declaratory and not imprecatory, where Gill takes them as requests and Wesley allows that some may be both prophecies and prayers
Calvin answers the objection that we are bidden to pray for our enemies by saying that the prayer is not indiscriminate but against the reprobate who were perpetual enemies of the Church
Gill reports a comparison with an Arabic word meaning madness, which would make the sorrow of heart a distraction of mind
themes: Sitting and rising taken for the whole of a life
A pertinacity in enemies that becomes a ground of hope
An alphabet counted three times over to sixty-six
Destruction asked for as testimony that God sits in heaven
